title: Given the head of a singly linked list, determine whether it reads the same forward and backward. Aim for linear time and constant extra space. (LeetCode: Palindrome Linked List)
shortTitle: Palindrome LinkedList (Find Middle, Reverse Half, Compare)
keyPoints: Find the middle with fast-slow pointers, reverse the second half in place, then compare both halves node by node.
Optionally reverse the second half again to restore the list and avoid side effects.
The technique runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
The naive approach copies values into an array and checks with two pointers, using O(n) extra space.
Odd-length lists are handled naturally because the single middle node has no partner to compare.
In production, always restore the list after checking to avoid corrupting shared data.

s1_definition.oneliner: Find the middle, reverse the second half, compare the two halves, then optionally reverse back.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Palindrome check** – determine whether a linked list reads the same forward and backward.
- **Step 1** – find the middle using fast-slow pointers.
- **Step 2** – reverse the second half in place.
- **Step 3** – compare the first half and reversed second half node by node.
- **Step 4** – restore the second half by reversing it again (production best practice).
- **Complexity** – O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh has a chain of linked digits forming a cheque security code and wants to know if it reads the same from either end. He finds the middle of the chain, flips the second half around, walks both halves comparing digit by digit, and then flips the second half back to leave the chain unchanged.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
List: 1 -> 2 -> 2 -> 1

Step 1: Find middle (slow/fast)
  slow: 1 -> 2 -> [2]     (lands on second 2)
  fast: 1 -> 2 -> null     (reached end)

Step 2: Reverse second half starting at slow
  Before: ... -> 2 -> 1 -> null
  After:  null <- 2 <- 1   (reversed head = 1)

Step 3: Compare
  First half:   1 -> 2
  Reversed half: 1 -> 2
  1 == 1  ✓
  2 == 2  ✓
  Reversed pointer is null -> stop -> PALINDROME

Step 4: Restore second half
  Before: null <- 2 <- 1
  After:  ... -> 2 -> 1 -> null  (original order)
```

```text
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│      Palindrome Linked List Flow              │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                              │
│   1. Fast-slow pointers -> find middle       │
│              │                               │
│              ▼                               │
│   2. Reverse second half in place            │
│              │                               │
│              ▼                               │
│   3. Walk first half + reversed half         │
│      Compare values node by node             │
│              │                               │
│         Mismatch?                            │
│      Yes: NOT palindrome                     │
│      No:  IS palindrome                      │
│              │                               │
│              ▼                               │
│   4. Reverse second half again (restore)     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Checking whether a linked list is a palindrome in constant space combines three fundamental techniques. Find the middle with fast-slow pointers, reverse the second half in place, compare both halves node by node, and restore the second half.

The naive approach copies values into an array and checks with two indices, which is clear but uses O(n) space. The in-place approach avoids that allocation entirely, which matters for long lists in memory-sensitive services.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh verified symmetric reference codes stored as linked chains of digits. The chains could be long and the service was memory-sensitive, so the in-place approach met the constant-space requirement. The original chain was used by the next step in the flow, so restoring it was not optional.

The senior-level point is the restoration. Reversing the second half mutates the list, so in any shared or concurrent context, restore it afterward or document that the method is destructive. Being able to compose find-middle, reverse, and compare into one clean solution demonstrates production-level thinking.

Remember one sentence: find the middle, reverse the second half, compare node by node, and restore the list.
